finding.claim: deleteAccount never enforces the authorization check: canDelete(u, a) is called at line 22 but its boolean result is discarded, so any caller can delete any account by id (IDOR / broken access control).
finding.source: long id from the DELETE /accounts/{id} path parameter (comment at line 19), supplied by any caller; User u supplied by the caller, identity verification not in this repo.
finding.sink: accounts.remove(id) at line 23 (deletion of the account record).

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) receives caller's user and target id.
Account a = accounts.get(id) loads target account.
canDelete(u, a) evaluated but result discarded; no throw, no branch.
canDelete = u.admin() || a.ownerId() == u.id(); correct but unused here.
closeAccount calls assertCanDelete(u, a) before removal; deleteAccount omits this enforcement, indicating the bug.

finding.guards_checked: canDelete (lines 9-11) not enforced; assertCanDelete (lines 13-17) not called in deleteAccount; no other files in repo (no routers, filters, or tests) provide an upstream enforcement. Mitigation may exist outside this repo and should be verified.

verdict.guard_found: None effective in the repo. canDelete (src/AccountService.java:9-11) returns a bool, but its result is discarded as a bare statement at line 22. assertCanDelete (lines 13-17) is never called in deleteAccount; it is only used by closeAccount at line 29. accounts.remove(id) at line 23 runs unconditionally. The repo contains only this one file, so no router, filter, or authentication layer is visible here.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the source: canDelete's boolean is discarded at src/AccountService.java:22 and accounts.remove(id) runs unconditionally at line 23, while closeAccount at line 29 enforces the same check via assertCanDelete. Any caller who can reach deleteAccount with a User (an authenticated low-privilege user is the realistic attacker) can delete another user's account. The only remaining uncertainty is whether a router outside this repo blocks that call, which the repo cannot show, but no control in the code blocks it.

finding.claim: For a nonexistent id, accounts.get returns null; canDelete then dereferences a.ownerId() for non-admin callers, throwing NullPointerException (admin callers silently no-op). closeAccount has the same behavior via assertCanDelete (line 29).
finding.source: long id from the caller (path parameter, attacker-controlled).
finding.sink: NullPointerException at line 10 (a.ownerId()) reached via line 22 (deleteAccount) and line 29 (closeAccount); observable as differing responses between admin and non-admin callers.

trace.note: accounts.get(id) returns null for unknown id.
non-admin: a.ownerId() dereferences null -> NPE; admin: short-circuits to true.
closeAccount same pattern via assertCanDelete at line 29.

finding.guards_checked: No null check on a before canDelete/assertCanDelete. Exception-to-response mapping is outside this repo and unverified.

verdict.guard_found: none. There is no null check on `a` before canDelete at src/AccountService.java:22 or assertCanDelete at line 29. canDelete (line 10) dereferences a.ownerId() when u is not admin, so the NPE is thrown before any result is used.
verdict.reason: The trace holds: accounts.get(id) returns null (line 21/28), and for a non-admin caller canDelete dereferences a.ownerId() at line 10, throwing NPE, while admin short-circuits at line 10 and the call proceeds. The attacker is any authenticated low-privilege user who can supply an arbitrary id, so the claim is reachable. Impact is low (an existence oracle via differing error responses, whose observability depends on the unverified exception mapping), and the finding misses a larger issue: deleteAccount at line 22 discards canDelete's boolean result, so any authenticated user can delete any existing account.
